1016.title: Infinite spaces
1016.hook: Pascal: the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me
1016.howItsDone: Readers of Pascal's Pensées, Christian and otherwise, return to his fragments on the infinite spaces and the thinking reed when they think about the human place in a vast universe.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was furuike, Basho's old pond. Your line was the sound of water. Today a new stretch begins: philosophers, poets and scientists.

Away from the city lights, on a clear night, the sky stops being a ceiling. It opens. The stars aren't painted on anything. They're out there, at distances you can't hold in your head, and between them is dark, and the dark goes on. Some people feel wonder at that. Some feel a cold drop in the stomach. Most of this block has been about the first feeling. Today is about the second, from Blaise Pascal, a French thinker who wrote it down in one short line.
screen: `THE SKY STOPS BEING A CEILING.` → `WONDER, OR A COLD DROP.` → `BLAISE PASCAL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In his Pensées, a word that means thoughts, Pascal writes, in Trotter's translation: "The eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me." Not delights. Frightens. It's an honest place for awe to begin. The sky doesn't answer. It doesn't even notice. Second, where we stand. Elsewhere in the same book, Pascal asks what a human being is in nature, and answers with a riddle: nothing compared to the infinite, everything compared to nothing, somewhere in the middle between the two. Third, the reed. Then Pascal writes, again in Trotter's words: "Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed." A vapor, a drop of water, he goes on, could kill us. And yet if the universe crushed us, we would still be nobler than the thing that killed us, because we know we die, and the universe knows nothing of it. Fourth, who's frightened. Readers disagree about whose voice the frightened line is. Some hear Pascal himself, a man of Christian faith, being honest about his fear. Others hear him speaking in the voice of a doubter he hoped to reach. Either way, look at the shape of it. The silent spaces are vast, and they know nothing. The small, frightened one under them is the only one in the picture who knows anything at all.
screen: `ETERNAL SILENCE. INFINITE SPACES.` · `NOTHING, EVERYTHING, AND THE MIDDLE.` · `A THINKING REED.` · `THE UNIVERSE KNOWS NOTHING OF IT.` · then, large: `THE SILENT SPACES.`

segments.voice: Look out at the night if it's dark, or close your eyes and recall the darkest, clearest sky you've seen, and let your gaze go past the nearest star to the dark behind it, feeling the size of it even if it's uncomfortable. Then notice the one doing the looking, breathing, small, aware, and hold both together. If you pray, you can bring the silence and the fear as they are.
Infinite spaces. Pascal's line: the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me. Awe with its cold side showing. Today's word.
Your line: the silent spaces. Vast and knowing nothing, and under them, a thinking reed. Day one thousand sixteen.

1017.title: Two things
1017.hook: Kant: the starry heavens above and the moral law within fill the mind with awe
1017.howItsDone: Readers of Kant often meet this passage on its own, and some people who keep a reflective practice pair a look at the night sky with an evening review of their own conduct.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascal under the night sky, and the silence of the infinite spaces that frightened him. Your line was the silent spaces. Today a second philosopher looks at the same sky and finds a second thing to set beside it.

Two directions. Up, where the stars are. And in, where a sense of duty says: this must be done. Immanuel Kant spent a whole book on duty and reason, argued step by careful step. Then, in its conclusion, he stops arguing and writes something closer to a confession. Two things, he says, fill the mind with admiration and awe, and the feeling grows the more often and the more steadily we think about them. The starry heavens above. And the moral law within.
screen: `UP, WHERE THE STARS ARE.` → `IN, WHERE DUTY SPEAKS.` → `TWO THINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the pairing. Stars are easy to stand in awe of. Kant sets beside them something that doesn't shine at all: the sense, inside a person, that some things must be done and some must not, whatever they cost. He says he doesn't have to hunt for either one as if it were hidden in darkness. He sees them both in front of him, and ties them straight to the awareness of his own existence. Second, the sky. The view of a countless crowd of worlds, Kant says, seems to wipe out his importance, as a creature of matter who must give that matter back to the planet he stands on. Pascal felt that smallness as fear. Kant names it plainly and doesn't look away. Third, the law within. Here the arithmetic flips. The same person who shrinks under the stars is raised up by the moral law, given a worth that doesn't depend on size, or the body, or the world of things. Fourth, the growing. A view seen every day can wear thin. Kant claims the opposite for these two: the oftener and the more steadily you reflect, the more they fill the mind. Some readers hear in that a practice, not just a feeling: looking up, and looking in, every day, and finding they don't wear out.
screen: `TWO THINGS: ABOVE AND WITHIN` · `THE STARS MAKE A PERSON SMALL` · `THE LAW WITHIN MAKES A PERSON LARGE` · `AWE THAT GROWS WITH LOOKING` · then, large: `ABOVE AND WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Look up first, at the sky through a window or outside, or at whatever is above you, and let it be bigger than you are. Then close your eyes and turn the same attention inward: is there one thing you already know is right to do, a call owed, a truth to tell, a kindness put off? Don't argue with it; just look at it, the way you looked at the sky.
Two things. Kant's pair: the starry heavens above, the moral law within, and the awe that grows the longer you look at them. Today's word.
Your line: above and within. The stars shrink you, and the law within lifts you back up. Day one thousand seventeen, done.

1018.title: A presence
1018.hook: Wordsworth felt a presence that disturbed him with joy
1018.carry: a joy strong enough to unsettle
1018.tomorrow: A world in a grain of sand
1018.howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path keep a habit of slow walks outdoors, and readers of Wordsworth often return to this passage from Tintern Abbey as a way of naming moments of awe in nature.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kant's two things: the starry heavens above and the moral law within. Your line was above and within. Today a poet walks back into a valley and meets something he can't quite name.

"Five years have past; five summers, with the length of five long winters!" That's how the poem opens. William Wordsworth is back on the banks of the river Wye, a few miles above Tintern Abbey, looking at a landscape he last saw five years before. Same cliffs, same quiet, same smoke rising from the trees. But he isn't the same, and the poem is about the difference. When he tries to say what this place has given him, what comes out isn't a view at all. It's a presence.
screen: `FIVE YEARS HAVE PAST.` → `THE SAME VALLEY.` → `A DIFFERENT MAN.`

segments.voice: Here are his words: "And I have felt a presence that disturbs me with the joy of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime of something far more deeply interfused, whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, and the round ocean and the living air, and the blue sky, and in the mind of man". First, the odd verb. The presence disturbs him, and what it disturbs him with is joy. Not calm, not comfort: a joy strong enough to unsettle. Kant spoke of admiration and awe; Wordsworth adds that awe can shake a person, even when it's glad. Second, interfused. The presence isn't standing outside the world, looking in. It's mixed through things, the way light is mixed through air. Third, the address list: setting suns, the round ocean, the living air, the blue sky. Ordinary things anyone can see on a clear evening. Fourth, the last stop: the mind of man. The same presence that lives in the sunset lives in the one watching it. And notice what Wordsworth never does in these lines. He doesn't give it a name. He says presence. He says something. Some readers hear God in it; some hear nature; some hear both. The poem leaves it unnamed, and seems to want it that way.
screen: `A JOY THAT DISTURBS` · `SOMETHING DEEPLY INTERFUSED` · `SUNSETS, OCEAN, AIR, SKY` · `AND IN THE MIND` · then, large: `A PRESENCE.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly outdoors at half your normal speed, or slowly across a room, or stand at an open window. Don't look for anything in particular; let the light, the air and the sky do what they do. If a moment stirs you a little, let it, and if nothing comes, that's part of it too.
A presence. Wordsworth's name for something he couldn't name, living in sunsets, ocean, air and sky, and in the mind that sees them. Today's word.
Your line: a joy strong enough to unsettle. Wordsworth never named it, and he didn't need to. See you tomorrow.

1019.title: A world in a grain of sand
1019.hook: Blake: see a world in a grain of sand
1019.howItsDone: Some people on a personal spiritual path practice close looking at one small object, a seed, a stone, a grain, as a short daily meditation, and Blake's opening lines are often read alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wordsworth's presence, living in sunsets and sky and the mind that sees them. Your line was a joy strong enough to unsettle. Today the awe shrinks down to something you could lose under a fingernail.

Pour a little salt onto a dark table. Each grain is tiny and rough-edged, easy never to give a second look. The last few days have been about big things: infinite spaces, the starry heavens, the round ocean. Today a poet points the other way. William Blake begins a poem not with the sky but with the smallest thing on a beach, and says the whole world is in it. Not a picture of the world. The world.
screen: `A LITTLE SALT ON A DARK TABLE.` → `FROM THE STARS TO A GRAIN.` → `THE WORLD IS IN IT.`

segments.voice: Here are the opening lines of Blake's Auguries of Innocence: "To see a World in a Grain of Sand and a Heaven in a Wild Flower, Hold Infinity in the palm of your hand and Eternity in an hour." Four pairs, each small beside large. First, a world in a grain. Notice the verb: to see. Blake isn't making a claim about sand. He's describing a way of looking, close enough and long enough that the small thing opens. Second, a heaven in a wild flower. Not a garden rose: a wild one, the kind nobody planted and nobody waters. Third, infinity in your hand, eternity in an hour. The biggest things there are, set inside a palm and a single hour. Some readers hear a promise that the ordinary day is big enough. Fourth, the part that's easy to miss: the poem keeps going, in a long run of couplets, and many aren't about beauty at all. They're about harm, to caged birds, starved dogs, hunted hares, and to people too. The very first: "A Robin Red breast in a Cage puts all Heaven in a Rage." The same seeing that finds heaven in a flower finds heaven's anger at a caged bird. If a grain holds a world, a small cruelty isn't small either. The tiny thing is holy, and so the tiny wrong matters.
screen: `A WORLD IN A GRAIN` · `A HEAVEN IN A WILD FLOWER` · `INFINITY IN YOUR HAND` · `SMALL THINGS MATTER BOTH WAYS` · then, large: `A WORLD IN A GRAIN.`

segments.voice: Put one small thing on your palm or on something dark: a grain of rice, salt or sand, a seed, a crumb of soil. Look only at it, its edges, its color, whether it catches light, and when the mind wanders, bring it back to the grain. You don't have to see a world; just keep looking, and see what the looking does.
Blake. The poet whose way of seeing holds a world in a grain of sand, a heaven in a wild flower, and finds that small harms matter too. Today's word.
Your line: a world in a grain. Blake's way of seeing cuts both ways. That's day one thousand nineteen.

1020.title: Charged with grandeur
1020.hook: Hopkins: the world is charged with the grandeur of God
1020.howItsDone: Christians who love poetry often read God's Grandeur as a prayer of praise, and people on a personal spiritual path use its images of shaken foil and deep-down freshness as a prompt for noticing beauty in worn, everyday places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Blake's grain of sand, with a world inside it. Your line was a world in a grain. Today a poet says the whole world is about to flash.

Hold a sheet of kitchen foil near a window and give it a shake. For a split second it throws light everywhere, then goes dull again. Gerard Manley Hopkins used that exact picture, shaken foil, in a short poem about God and the world. He was a Christian poet and a Jesuit priest, and his poem names God in its first line and the Holy Ghost in its closing lines. Between them, he says the world is like that foil. Shake it, and it flashes. It's charged.
screen: `SHAKEN FOIL, FLASHING.` → `GOD IN THE FIRST LINE.` → `THE WORLD IS CHARGED.`

segments.voice: The poem is God's Grandeur, and it opens: "The world is charged with the grandeur of God. It will flame out, like shining from shook foil". First, charged. A charged thing is loaded, ready to go off, like a storm cloud before lightning. Hopkins doesn't say grandeur sits in the world quietly. It's packed in, waiting to break out. Second, two ways it breaks out. It flames out, sudden, like the foil. And it "gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil crushed": slow and heavy, the way oil seeps from something pressed. Third, the honest middle. Hopkins doesn't pretend the world is all shining: "Generations have trod, have trod, have trod; and all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil". The soil is bare, and feet in shoes, he says, can't even feel it anymore. Fourth, the turn: "And for all this, nature is never spent; there lives the dearest freshness deep down things". Not on the surface. Deep down. The poem closes with its reason: "Because the Holy Ghost over the bent world broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings." For Hopkins the freshness has a source, and he names it in the language of his Christian faith. Some readers who don't share that faith still come back to the first two images: a world that flashes, and a world that seeps.
screen: `CHARGED: LOADED, READY TO FLASH` · `FLAME OUT, OOZE OF OIL` · `SEARED WITH TRADE` · `FRESHNESS DEEP DOWN THINGS` · then, large: `CHARGED.`

segments.voice: Look slowly around for anything that catches the light, a glass, a leaf, a drop of water, someone's hair, and when you find it, watch how the light moves as you move your head a little. If nothing flashes, look for the slow kind instead, something quietly lovely that's been there all along. If you pray, you can let the poem's first line be your prayer.
shook foil. Hopkins's image, from God's Grandeur, for the world's grandeur flashing out all at once, like sudden light. Today's word.

1021.title: The journeywork of the stars
1021.hook: Whitman: a leaf of grass is no less than the journeywork of the stars
1021.howItsDone: Readers of Whitman often return to Song of Myself on walks outdoors, and some people on a personal spiritual path use his lists of small creatures as a prompt to look at ordinary living things as finished, careful work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hopkins's shook foil, the world's grandeur ready to flame out. Your line was charged. Today, a single blade of grass.

A child runs up with two fistfuls of grass and asks: what is it? That's a scene from Walt Whitman's Song of Myself: "A child said What is the grass? fetching it to me with full hands; how could I answer the child? I do not know what it is any more than he." A grown man, stumped by a handful of grass. Later in the same poem, he gives an answer you won't find in any botany book.
screen: `WHAT IS THE GRASS?` → `I DO NOT KNOW.` → `AN ANSWER LATER ON.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "I believe a leaf of grass is no less than the journey-work of the stars, and the pismire is equally perfect, and a grain of sand, and the egg of the wren". First, no less than. Whitman isn't saying grass is a little bit wonderful. He's saying it equals the stars' own work. Journeywork is an old craft word for work done by a trained hand, so in Whitman's picture a single blade is something the stars made, and made well. Second, the list keeps going. The pismire, an old word for an ant, is "equally perfect". So is a grain of sand, which we met with Blake, and the egg of the wren. Whitman piles them up so nothing gets ranked lower. Third, the next line: "And the tree-toad is a chef-d'oeuvre for the highest". Chef-d'oeuvre is French for masterpiece. And then, "the running blackberry would adorn the parlors of heaven". A bramble from a ditch, good enough for heaven's living room. Fourth, the first two words: I believe. Whitman doesn't claim to have measured this. He states it as belief, just as the child's question got no measured answer. Wonder, for him, starts with admitting he doesn't know what grass is, and ends with refusing to call any of it small.
screen: `NO LESS THAN THE STARS` · `THE ANT IS EQUALLY PERFECT` · `A MASTERPIECE FOR THE HIGHEST` · `I BELIEVE` · then, large: `JOURNEYWORK OF THE STARS.`

segments.voice: Pick a single blade of grass, or kneel and look at one where it grows; if there's none nearby, a houseplant leaf, a kitchen herb or a weed in a crack will do. Look at its edges, its veins, the way it narrows to a point, and turn it in the light. No need to think anything grand: just look at it as if someone skilled had made it.

1022.title: The transparent eyeball
1022.hook: Emerson, on a bare common at twilight, feels himself become nothing and see all
1022.howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often meet this passage from Nature as a description of awe outdoors, and some people on a personal spiritual path practice standing still in open spaces, attention turned outward, as a short daily discipline.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Whitman's leaf of grass, no less than the journeywork of the stars. Your line was journeywork of the stars. Today ends the week, with a man crossing a muddy field at dusk.

Snow puddles. A bare town common. Twilight, and a cloudy sky. Nothing special happening. Here's how Ralph Waldo Emerson describes it in his book Nature: "Crossing a bare common, in snow puddles, at twilight, under a clouded sky, without having in my thoughts any occurrence of special good fortune, I have enjoyed a perfect exhilaration. I am glad to the brink of fear." No mountaintop. No good news. Wet feet. A few sentences on, his thoughts gone to the woods, he reaches for a very strange picture.
screen: `SNOW PUDDLES AT TWILIGHT.` → `NO SPECIAL GOOD FORTUNE.` → `A PERFECT EXHILARATION.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "Standing on the bare ground, my head bathed by the blithe air, and uplifted into infinite space, all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all". First, the ordinary setting. Emerson goes out of his way to say nothing lucky had happened. The joy comes from bare ground and open air, not from his day going well. Second, glad to the brink of fear. Pascal's spaces frightened him; Wordsworth's presence disturbed him with joy. Emerson's gladness comes right up to fear and stops there. Third, what disappears. Not Emerson himself: what vanishes is "mean egotism", the small, grasping self that keeps score. With that gone, "I am nothing; I see all". A transparent eye doesn't look at itself. It only lets the world through. Fourth, the week. Seven people, seven ways of looking. Pascal and the silent spaces. Kant's two things, above and within. Wordsworth's presence. Blake's world in a grain. Hopkins and a world charged. Whitman's grass, the journeywork of the stars. And Emerson, nothing, seeing all. Some of them name God, as Emerson does a few words later, calling himself "part or particle of God". Some leave the name out. Each stood still long enough for something to come through.
screen: `NO SPECIAL GOOD FORTUNE` · `GLAD TO THE BRINK OF FEAR` · `I AM NOTHING; I SEE ALL` · `A WEEK OF LOOKING UP` · then, large: `NOTHING, SEEING ALL.`

segments.voice: Stand still in an open space, a yard, a balcony, or a doorway with the sky in it, arms loose, and let the air touch your face. Let your attention go outward only: what you see, what you hear, what you feel on your skin. Each time a thought about yourself comes up, a plan, a worry, a score, notice it, and turn back to seeing.
